### Observed differences

- Resource assignment changed for six activities (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22). In the earlier window, each of these activities was handled by one group of resources — for example, User_51 received about 13 in 100 assignments of A22, about 8 in 100 of A01 and A03, and about 7 in 100 of A17. In the later window, a largely different group dominates: User_24 received about 11 in 100 assignments of A22, and User_76 about 8–9 in 100 of A13, A14 and A17, while User_51 no longer appears among the ten most used resources for any of these activities. The overlap between the two groups is small; only a few resources keep visible shares in both windows. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- This is a replacement of which resources do the work, not a change in concentration: the share going to resources outside the ten most used stayed similar (about 40–50 in 100 before, about 38–47 in 100 after), and the same resources lose share in all six activities while the same others gain. Profile dissimilarity is about 0.39–0.53, each difference was exceeded in fewer than about 1 in 1000 random re-splits, and the profiles rest on many observations (200 of 200 traces for A01, 199 of 200 for A03, about 300 assignments each for A13 and A14, about 275 for A17, about 125 for A22). [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- A13 and A14 show identical before and after profiles and identical support counts, so they most likely reflect one underlying difference rather than two independent ones. [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004]
- In control flow, A18's outgoing transitions shifted: in the earlier window about 53 in 100 of its observed outgoing transitions led to A22 and about 33 in 100 to A10 (A03 and A12 about 7 each); in the later window about 69 in 100 led to A10, about 6 to A22, and transitions to A02 and A16 appeared at about 12–13 in 100 each. This rests on only about 15–16 observed outgoing transitions per window, so it is weakly grounded. [DIR001]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports a change in resource allocation: in the later window, the work on activities A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 was reassigned from one group of resources to a largely different group — the previous handlers (including User_51) dropped out of the most-used set while a new set (including User_24 and User_76) took over, with the overall spread across many resources unchanged. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

The support rests on the resources family producing six qualifying items where about 0.005 were expected by chance without a change — a count many times larger than an unchanged process would yield — together with the same direction of shift in all six items, large observation counts behind each profile, and differences larger than in about 999.5 of 1000 random re-splits. Limitations: resource codes are anonymous, so no roles, people or teams can be inferred; A13 and A14 likely describe a single underlying difference; and the evidence shows only that assignment shares changed, not how the new shares came about. A competing explanation the evidence cannot rule out is that the two windows simply contain different sets of active resources (for example because they cover different periods), which would produce the same profile replacement without any reallocation of these specific activities. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

Other differences: the shift in A18's successor mix (from mostly A22 to mostly A10, with A02 and A16 newly observed) is not part of the main hypothesis: the control-flow family produced one item where about 0.17 were expected by chance — a level an unchanged process typically produces — and the profile is based on only about 15–16 observed outgoing transitions per window, so sampling variation cannot be excluded. [DIR001]
